text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Wednesday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Namibia's bid to have its elephant population downgraded at the upcoming CITES conference has received a significant boost. Traffic, the wildlife trade monitoring programme of the World Wide Fund for Nature and the World Conservation Union, has announced its qualified backing for the proposals of Namibia, Zimbabwe and Botswana to have their elephant populations moved from Appendix one to Appendix two. The organisation supports trade in live animals and hunting trophies, but not elephant ivory or hides for the time being.

- The chairman of Namibia's meat board has been given a seven-day ultimatum to resign or face dismissal following charges of withholding statutory funds from the Namibia National Farmers Union. This was confirmed byAgriculture Minister Helmut Angula following cabinet decision to this effect two weeks ago.

- The United States has in principle agreed to finance a feasibility study for a railway connection between Namibia and Angola, after Washington had originlly withheld its support for the multi-million dollar project. The planned railway is to connect Tsumeb with Ondangwa and Oshikango in the north of the country, and then link up with the existing railway line from the Angolan harbour of Namibe to Menongue in the southeastern province of Cuando-Cubango.

- Ten luxury inter-continental planes in the price range of N$130 million to N$200 million are in the running for the state tender for the substitution of the Falcon900B as presidential jet. According to deputy minister of transport, Dr Klaus Dierks, a final decision is to be taken within the next six weeks. Among the potential new jets are an American Gulfstream V, the new Falcon 900B from France, a new Global Express from Canada, and a smaller version of the Airbus, which is currently being developed by Boeing.

- The department of nature conservation of the Polytechnic of Namibia has agreed to start a project to study the behaviour of baboons within the capital city's perimeters and to find a solution to the tension between animal and man. During the past two years, during which Namibia experienced a ravaging drought, baboons repeatedly entered residential areas and frightened residents.
